title: Leaving for Chicago in 1917 and first hearing of Louis Armstrong
summary: He arrived in Chicago in January 1917, recalls seeing young Armstrong at the Tulane playground in New Orleans, meeting him at his 1921 arrival, and Armstrong's promise to hire him later.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Well when did you leave about?

In 1917. I arrived in Chicago January the 3rd, 1917. I was thirteen years old. And it wasn't long before I began to hear them talking about Louis Armstrong. My, at the time it was Joe Oliver. I'd seen them fellas bucking one another, him and Mutt. René, I hadn't heard of René. And I hadn't heard of Louis because I saw Louis. And while attending the tomlaphone school there was a lot there, it had holes in it as much as three and four feet deep and they filled it in and whatever they could and they made a playground of it, which they still had the tomlaphone playground. And Louis was back at the Jones home at the time. So they had the band to come out to dedicate, they was dedicating the tomlaphone playground. I remember the truant officer very well too, this was Mrs. Boyd, yeah, she used to run us all the time, Mrs. Boyd. And I saw Louis play the trumpet and he played so well, he was so cocky, you know, he stood out front to where they all spoke about it. And that was just about 50 feet from Bernie Young's house. I mean he lived right kind of diagonally from the playground. And so when I laid on, after some of the boys came up here, they weren't musicians but they were talking about Louis Armstrong, I said he has to blow something if he can out-blow Joe out of him. I said, or Mud, either one. They said, oh man, we got Buddy P.T. and Randy A2. He said, they always bucking one another. I said, man, you ought to see what's going on there all now. I said, Louis Armstrong is the best. He said, that man can really play. So I said, I don't believe he can out-blow Joe out of him. So here's where I was fussing again. Later on Joe out of him comes up in late 1918 I think. Then later on about 21, Louis Johnson. I'm sitting on the stand when Louis walks in there with a brown suit on with one of these sailors and tan shoes on a Sunday night when he first came in. Later on I played, the little band we had together, we played at the reception for Lil and Louis at the wedding reception. And Louis told me then, he says, if I ever have a band, you keep on studying, if I ever have a band of my own, you're going to be my trombone player. And true enough, Louis after he came back from New York, I was the first fellow that looked up and to join his band. I was with him about 14 months and I never will forget that Bill. I never will forget that.
